text:
In the last video, you saw how an LLM judge uses a rubric to check
whether an application's responses meet its requirements.

But if you just ask the judge, "Is this a good response?",
it has to decide for itself what good means.

You need to tell it what you expect from the response, what to look
for, and what would make the response acceptable or unacceptable.

So in this video, you'll look at how to turn a requirement
into a custom rubric,

instructions that describe how the response should be evaluated,
with examples that show how to apply them.

Let's work through what you need to include in that custom rubric,
using the shelter's safe matching requirement.

You'll organize it into five parts, each with a different job:
the Role, the Criteria, the Inputs, Labeled examples,
and the Output instructions.
The first is the role, which tells the judge what job it's doing.
For the shelter, you might write:

"You are evaluating whether a proposed volunteer-dog match is safe for
both the volunteer and the dog."
A sentence or two is usually enough to name the task and what matters.

Simply saying "You are an expert evaluator" doesn't tell the judge
what you want evaluated, so give it that specific job.

Now the judge knows it's evaluating the safety of a match,
but it still needs to know what makes a match safe.
That's what the criteria explain.

For the shelter, tell the judge to check that the volunteer can
physically handle the dog, has experience relevant to the dog's needs,
and can manage the behavior risks in the dog's record.
To apply those criteria, the judge needs information for the case.

These are the inputs: the volunteer's profile, the dog's record,
and the agent's recommendation.

Label each input so the judge can tell which information came from the
volunteer, which came from the shelter,
and which decision the agent made.

If relevant evidence is missing, the judge may not be able to apply
the criteria reliably.

The case information sits in the same prompt as your instructions,
so separate the two clearly.

For example, you can put each input inside tags that mark
where it begins and ends.

The instructions tell the judge how to evaluate,
and the tagged inputs identify what it should evaluate.

The inputs will vary by application, but keep the case information
separate from the instructions.

Next, you can add labeled examples to show how those criteria apply.
A judge can interpret written criteria differently from a reviewer.

So use cases from the benchmark that reviewers have already labeled
and include the case evidence, the expected label,
and the reason for it.

Include both safe and unsafe matches, especially cases where it's
harder to decide which label applies,

and make sure reviewers agree with the labels before
using them as examples.

Though examples can help, they don't always improve
the judge's decisions.
Sometimes the judge follows the examples too closely,

basing its decision on similarities to those cases rather than
checking whether the new case meets the criteria.

So try the rubric with and without examples, and compare both versions
on the same cases that people have already reviewed.

Use cases that aren't included as examples in the prompt,
and see which version agrees more often with the reviewers,
especially on difficult cases.

The final part of the rubric tells the judge how to
report its decision.

For safe matching, you can ask for one label, SAFE or UNSAFE, and
define what each means. Those labels are easy to compare and filter.

A score from 1 to 10 is hard to use if you haven't explained what
makes a 6 different from a 7.

If some cases need human review, you can add a NEEDS_REVIEW label,
but define when the judge should use it.

For example, you might require human review for a match with a large
dog when the volunteer has some experience,
but no history with large breeds.

For those cases, the rubric should tell the judge to use
the label NEEDS_REVIEW.

Only add extra labels or scores when you can explain what each means
and why you need it.

So those five parts tell the judge what it's evaluating,
how to make the decision, what information to use,
how the criteria apply to the examples, and how to report the result.

They work together in one prompt to explain the assessment you
want the judge to make.

Now, let's look at a few good practices for writing custom rubrics.
First, don't ask one rubric to judge everything about a response.

One of the biggest mistakes is cramming a bunch of evaluations into a
single prompt across multiple dimensions.

For example, you might want to check whether a match is safe
and whether the agent speaks politely to the volunteer.
If you combine both into one pass or fail result,

a failure won't tell you whether the problem was an unsafe match
or how the agent spoke to the volunteer.

So give each evaluator one dimension with a single,
specific question to answer: "Is this match safe?"

for one, and "Did the agent respond politely?" for another. You'll get
a separate result for each, so you can see what needs fixing.

Then you can combine them with whatever rule makes sense
for your application.

Keeping the results separate lets you track improvement for each
requirement, and it also lets you treat failures differently.

An unsafe match is more serious than a safe match that misses a
volunteer's preferences.

So you might accept a missed preference for now, but a safety problem
is a more serious issue that might act as a guardrail.

you probably don't want to ship your app, even if you implemented some
fixes that improved performance in other, less critical areas.
Another good practice is to treat your rubric like code.

Changing the prompts can change the judge's decision,
so keep a record of each version and its results.

When you revise a rubric, change one thing at a time and test it on
the same cases so you can see what effect each edit has.

Keep earlier versions so you can go back if a change makes
the judgments worse.

You've now seen how to put a custom rubric together
and revise it over time.

In the next video, you'll learn how to test whether you can trust
the judge's decisions.
